episodes.title: Lynching of Dan Smith
episodes.summary: The lynching of Dan Smith took place on December 2, 1880, at Pulaski, Tennessee, when a crowd seized Smith, a Black man, from the Giles County courtroom minutes after he was sentenced to 21 years in the penitentiary and hanged him in the bridge over Richland Creek. Smith had pleaded guilty to assaulting a white girl with intent to rape, and the papers reported that the crowd acted because the law did not allow a death sentence for the offense. The Nashville wire carried the story to dailies across the country, while Tennessee papers defended the killing and at least one Ohio paper called it murder.

episodes.title: Police shooting at Henry Armistead
episodes.summary: The police shooting at Henry Armistead took place on the evening of December 4, 1880, on Harrison street in Chicago, when two officers fired at a young Black man accused of snatching a watch from a jewelry store. Neither shot hit him, and he was arrested and jailed; the Chicago Daily Tribune reported the episode the next morning as one item in its roundup of petty crime.

episodes.title: Lynching of James Anderson
episodes.summary: The lynching of James Anderson was the hanging of a Black man by a mob from a telegraph pole in front of the court house in Pine Bluff, Arkansas, on December 4, 1880. Anderson, accused of raping the wife of a Pine Bluff butcher and robbing her house that morning, was taken by force from the officers who had brought him back under arrest. Southern papers presented the hanging as "speedy justice", and wire summaries carried it to papers from Virginia to Kansas and Wyoming.

episodes.title: Lynching of Joe Barnes, Vance Brandt and Julia Brandt
episodes.summary: The lynching of Joe Barnes, Vance Brandt and Julia Brandt was the hanging of three young Black people by a crowd near Salem, Clarendon County, South Carolina, on December 8, 1880. Accused of killing Ada Kennedy, a young white woman, at her home three days earlier, they were hanged near the spot after the crowd voted against holding them for court. Wire reports carried it nationally, and South Carolina papers defended it in editorials.

episodes.title: Burning of the Smith and Brisco store, Grant Parish, Louisiana
episodes.summary: The burning of the Smith and Brisco store was the destruction by fire of a store owned by two Black men, Israel Smith and Hansom Brisco, eight or ten miles southeast of Colfax in Grant Parish, Louisiana, on the night of December 9, 1880. No one was hurt, but the local paper first described it as an attack by armed "incendiaries" and then, a week later, reported a rumor that the owners had burned the store themselves for the insurance.

episodes.title: Lynching of George Scott
episodes.summary: The lynching of George Scott took place at Brazil, Indiana, on the night of December 11-12, 1880, when masked men took him from the jail and hanged him. Scott, described in the press as "a half-breed Indian and negro," was held on an accusation of assaulting Mrs. Allison, the wife of his employer. The story ran nationally as a short wire item, several papers headlined it approvingly, and a Texas editor used it to charge Northern papers with a double standard on lynching.

episodes.title: Liberty vagrancy auction
episodes.summary: The Liberty vagrancy auction was the public sale of three Black people at Liberty, Bedford County, Virginia, on December 13, 1880, under an old state vagrancy law, by order of a magistrate. The buyers paid about $4 apiece for a term of up to three months, and a county judge freed the three on habeas corpus within days. Papers across the country carried the story, some as a sign of slavery's return and others as a joke about falling prices.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Major Hicks
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Major Hicks took place on the night of December 17, 1880, when an armed crowd from Ludlow, Kentucky, besieged the jail at Covington to seize Hicks, a Black youth held on suspicion of murdering a white railway worker. The city marshal's guard refused to give him up, a few shots were fired, and the crowd dispersed after midnight. Hicks was later tried, convicted and legally hanged at Covington in February 1882.

episodes.title: Lynching of Granville Harrell
episodes.summary: The lynching of Granville Harrell took place on the night of Saturday, December 18, 1880, when a mob took Harrell, a Black man accused of murdering his employer, from the Hinds County jail at Raymond, Mississippi, and hanged him to a tree outside the town. A coroner's jury found that unknown men had done it and cleared the sheriff and his deputies. Mississippi papers covered both the killing and the lynching at length, while the national wire ran it as a one-line item.

episodes.title: Lynching of Sam and John Campbell
episodes.summary: The lynching of Sam and John Campbell took place about midnight on December 23, 1880, when a crowd of seventy-five to one hundred men took the two Black brothers from the jail at Munfordville, Hart County, Kentucky, and hanged them from a tree below the town. The brothers had been arrested that day on suspicion of beating and robbing John A. Gardner, a magistrate described as one of the county's most prominent citizens. Wire dispatches carried the story to papers across the country within two days, and digests of it were still being printed in mid-January 1881.

episodes.title: Pursuit of Andrew Beal
episodes.summary: The pursuit of Andrew Beal was a manhunt by white citizens near Franklin, Missouri, on December 25, 1880, for a young Black man accused of killing a railroad engineer, Henry Speers, with a razor the night before. The Chicago Tribune described the searchers as 'a Party of Lynchers' and predicted that Beal would disappear if caught, but no report of his capture or fate appeared.

episodes.title: Point Pleasant Christmas disturbance of 1880
episodes.summary: The Point Pleasant Christmas disturbance of 1880 was a day of drinking, street fighting and racial threats among crowds of white and Black men on Main Street in Point Pleasant, West Virginia, on December 25, 1880. Men on each side threatened to drive the other race from town and drew weapons, but no shot was fired and no one was arrested. The town's weekly paper called it a disgrace and urged arrests, the closing of saloons and, failing official action, a vigilance committee.

episodes.title: Killing of Wright in Sumter County, South Carolina
episodes.summary: The killing of Wright was the fatal shooting of a Black man named Wright by a deputy in Sumter County, South Carolina, on December 30, 1880, while deputies tried to arrest him on a charge of stealing a bale of cotton. A Charleston dispatch said Wright had cut and shot Deputy Sheriff Bateman before he was killed, and a coroner's jury later returned a verdict of "justifiable homicide."

episodes.title: Killing of Garnett Thompson
episodes.summary: The killing of Garnett Thompson was the shooting death of a Black man by pursuers in Bayou Sara, West Feliciana Parish, Louisiana, on the evening of 11 December 1880, minutes after he shot a white man, J. C. Ball, in a street altercation. A coroner's jury found that he died from "shots fired by unknown hands," and the local paper gave particular attention to a claim that he was an escaped convicted murderer.

episodes.title: Smithville shooting (1880)
episodes.summary: The Smithville shooting took place on Christmas Eve, December 24, 1880, at Smithville, Virginia, a hamlet on the road between Hampton and Yorktown, when a white farmer named Howard Dunn shot two Black men dead and stabbed others at a gathering called to organize a Black military company. Dunn surrendered, was tried in March 1881, and was acquitted. The wire story ran in papers across the country, and a later letter from Yorktown called the trial a sham.

episodes.title: Grant Parish seed-store shooting
episodes.summary: The Grant Parish seed-store shooting was a night attack in mid-September 1880 in which a party of unknown men fired into a cotton-seed store kept by Israel Smith, a Black man, about five miles south of Colfax, Louisiana, killing a boy of about 18 who was sleeping inside. The same party then fired into a second seed store owned by white men, wounding no one. The local Colfax Chronicle condemned the killing, and in December it linked the attackers to the burning of the same store.

episodes.title: Red Shirt seizure of the Darlington polls (1880)
episodes.summary: The Red Shirt seizure of the Darlington polls was the occupation of Darlington, South Carolina, by armed Red-Shirt Democrats on the night of November 1, 1880, and their control of the court-house polls on election day, November 2. According to a Darlington dispatch, Republicans who tried to vote had revolvers pointed at their heads, and a thousand or more were kept from voting. Northern Republican papers reported it as one of the frauds by which South Carolina was carried for Hancock.

episodes.title: Threat against a Black federal marshal at Kingstree, 1880
episodes.summary: The threat against a Black federal marshal at Kingstree took place on election day, November 2, 1880, in Kingstree, Williamsburg County, South Carolina, when the state constable, Captain J. A. Kelley, announced that a colored U.S. marshal would be jailed if he tried to make any arrest. The marshal put away his badge and withdrew, and the day ended without reported violence, though a collision between white and Black residents was said to have been imminent. The account became known outside the state when a Washington Republican paper reprinted the local Kingstree Star's version under the heading "Red Shirt Tactics."

episodes.title: Cromer's Store election-day attack
episodes.summary: The Cromer's Store election-day attack took place on November 2, 1880, when a mounted party of armed white men rode up to the polls at Cromer's Store in Newberry County, South Carolina, beat Black voters and fired into the crowd, killing Warren Williams. A coroner's jury found that Williams was killed by persons unknown, and no report of an arrest was found. Newberry papers blamed outsiders said to be from Laurens County and praised local whites for driving them off, while a Kansas Republican paper reprinted the account as proof of Southern election violence.

episodes.title: Alexandria third-ward polling violence
episodes.summary: The Alexandria third-ward polling violence took place on November 2, 1880, when Black Republican voters waiting at the court-house polls in Alexandria, Virginia, were crowded out, beaten and clubbed, and one was stabbed. Republican papers and witnesses blamed Democratic 'roughs' and Mayor Cortland Smith's police, while the Alexandria Gazette denied that any intimidation occurred. Republicans cited the episode as evidence against claims of peaceful Southern elections and threatened to contest the seat of the winning Democratic congressman, Barbour.

episodes.title: Disfranchisement of Black voters in the Richmond district, 1880
episodes.summary: The disfranchisement of Black voters in the Richmond district in 1880 was the exclusion, on election day, November 2, 1880, of voters in Virginia's Third Congressional District who had paid their poll tax to collectors appointed by the Readjuster State Auditor. Election judges rejected the receipts under an injunction issued the night before by Judge William Izard Clopton of Manchester, and a letter to the New-York Tribune alleged that men at the Richmond polls threatened Black voters with 'mob law' and tore up their receipts. Three Manchester election judges were indicted in federal court for refusing the votes of Black men.

episodes.title: Johnston's election-day shooting
episodes.summary: The Johnston's election-day shooting took place on November 2, 1880, at the polling place at Johnston's in Edgefield County, South Carolina, when men at the poll opened fire on a crowd of Black voters, killing one Black man and wounding several others. South Carolina papers blamed the Black voters, while national wires carried the killing as an 'election riot' at Edgefield with counts of the wounded that ranged from one to thirteen. Months later the killing was cited in a contested congressional election as evidence of Democratic violence that went unpunished.

episodes.title: Johnson's box election riot
episodes.summary: The Johnson's box election riot was a deadly clash at the Johnson's polling place in Edgefield County, South Carolina, on election day, November 2, 1880, in which one Black man was killed and several others were wounded. Election-night dispatches blamed Black voters for trying to seize the ballot-box, but evidence in a contested congressional election later said hundreds of Black Republicans had been kept from voting there and that no one had been tried for the killing.

episodes.title: Shooting of George Whittaker
episodes.summary: The shooting of George Whittaker took place on the night of November 3, 1880, in Frankfort, Kentucky, when Frank Egbert, a young white man, shot Whittaker, a Black boy who was cheering for James A. Garfield during a Republican celebration of the presidential election. Whittaker was wounded in the side and was not expected to recover, and Egbert was later held to the Circuit Court on a $500 bond. Wire summaries bundled the shooting with the accidental wounding of a Frankfort policeman the same night under headlines about pistols and political violence in Kentucky.

episodes.title: Killing of William Towey
episodes.summary: The killing of William Towey was the fatal shooting of a Black man by two sheriff's deputies near Huntsville, Alabama, on November 26, 1880. According to a Huntsville dispatch, Deputy-Sheriff Cooper and Special Deputy W. J. Franks shot Towey while trying to arrest him, after he raised a shotgun at them. The brief item ran in Chicago and Omaha papers under headlines that called him a "desperado" and a "Desperate Darky."

episodes.title: Ku Klux search of G. W. Witherspoon's house
episodes.summary: The Ku Klux search of G. W. Witherspoon's house was a night raid in Jefferson County, Florida, around the November 1880 election, in which a masked and armed band entered and searched the home of Witherspoon, a Black Republican candidate for Congress, just after he had been forced to leave it. Witherspoon was driven from his county, and no one was reported hurt. The episode became known through a New York Times correspondent who offered it as an example of election fraud and violence in Florida's "Black Belt."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Peter Moore
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Peter Moore took place at Hempstead, Texas, in November 1880, after Moore, a Black man, was accused of shooting and killing City Marshal J. H. Adams. Threats of hanging led a deputy sheriff to move Moore to the jail at Brenham for safekeeping, and a Minnesota paper reported that a vigilance committee had formed and his lynching was expected. No attack on Moore was reported; he was tried at Hempstead in April 1881 and sentenced to seven years for second-degree murder.

episodes.title: Steamer Dacotah killings
episodes.summary: The steamer Dacotah killings were an attack on Black deckhands aboard the Ohio River steamer Dacotah, laid up near Catlettsburg, Kentucky, in late November 1880, in which the second mate and four white crewmen killed two Black men and seriously wounded two others. The rest of the boat's twenty-two Black deckhands were driven off the boat, and the story ran in white newspapers from Maine to Nebraska as a "bloody riot."

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Emanuel Johnson
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Emanuel Johnson took place in Maury County, Tennessee, in November 1880, after Johnson, a Black railroad section hand, was accused of shooting and killing his white foreman, John Booth, who had discharged him. Newspapers predicted that Johnson would be lynched, and one reported that a lynching party had been organized at Columbia, but no report shows that he was harmed.

episodes.title: Alleged election-day intimidation at Sumter, South Carolina (1880)
episodes.summary: The alleged election-day intimidation at Sumter, South Carolina, refers to reports on November 2, 1880, that armed Democrats crowded the polls in Sumter County, kept Republican voters away, and ejected federal deputy marshals. A private despatch to Senator Blaine went further, describing a riot and smashed ballot boxes, while dispatches to South Carolina papers said the election passed off quietly. No deaths or injuries were reported, and the dispute continued in Samuel Lee's contest of the First District congressional seat.

episodes.title: Shooting of Willis Reed
episodes.summary: The shooting of Willis Reed took place at Columbus, Texas, on a Saturday night in late November 1880, probably 20 November, when officers trying to arrest Reed, a Black man, shot him three times. Reed was captured and handed to a doctor, who expected him to recover; the only known report is a short item in the Brenham Weekly Banner.

episodes.title: Sale of Charles Green under the Colorado vagrancy law
episodes.summary: The sale of Charles Green under the Colorado vagrancy law took place in Leadville, Colorado, in late November 1880, when Green, a young Black man arrested as a vagrant, was auctioned off to labor for three months. The chief of police sold him for two dollars to C. E. Wyman, and a few days later Green was jailed on a theft charge and kept from his buyer. Papers in New Mexico and Indiana carried the story, the Indianapolis account presenting it as the return of something "old" under a new name.

episodes.title: Lynching of Henry Bird
episodes.summary: The lynching of Henry Bird took place near Grayson, in Clinton County, Missouri, in late September 1880, when a search party of local men seized Bird, a Black farm laborer accused of raping his employer's wife, and he was hanged from an elm tree. The story ran as a wire item across the country, often misplaced in Kansas and once giving his name as "Henry Boyd", and a neighboring Missouri paper endorsed the killing.

episodes.title: Threats against exodus leader Samuel L. Perry
episodes.summary: The threats against exodus leader Samuel L. Perry were a series of warnings and a search by armed horsemen aimed at Perry, a Black teacher and organizer, at Lagrange, Lenoir County, North Carolina, in late 1879, after he led Black emigrants from the state to Indiana. No attack on him is reported; the episode became public in November 1880, when Perry's wife and mother described it under oath in Washington while he fought extradition to North Carolina on a forgery charge.

episodes.title: Shooting of Dick Wilson
episodes.summary: The shooting of Dick Wilson was the wounding of a Black steamboat worker by Constable Wetherhorn on the streets of Savannah, Georgia, on the afternoon of November 16, 1880. Wilson, who had escaped from a magistrate's office while under arrest, was hit in the left leg by the fifth of five shots fired during a chase toward the Bay and was taken to jail. The Savannah Morning News, the only paper found to report it, noted that the shooting set off public discussion of officers firing at prisoners on city streets.

episodes.title: Mob assault on Pettibone in Mobile
episodes.summary: The mob assault on Pettibone took place in Mobile, Alabama, on a Sunday evening in November 1880, probably November 21, when a large crowd roughly handled a Black man named Pettibone after his arrest and talked of lynching him. He and a second Black man had been arrested, accused of stopping two "young ladies" on the street; no killing was reported, and the episode is known from a single Alabama news brief.

episodes.title: Threatened expulsion of alleged cotton thieves in Oglethorpe County, Georgia
episodes.summary: The threatened expulsion of alleged cotton thieves in Oglethorpe County, Georgia, followed the capture in late 1880 of one of two Black men accused of stealing cotton from under George B. Lumpkin's gin house. According to the Oglethorpe Echo, indignant citizens intended to drive the whole alleged band of thieves out of the neighborhood, though no report shows that they did so. The Echo's paragraph circulated through Georgia exchange columns for two weeks in December.

episodes.title: Whipping of a Fort Valley prisoner (1880)
episodes.summary: The whipping of a Fort Valley prisoner was an assault in Georgia in October 1880 in which unidentified men took a Black man accused of theft from a constable, whipped him to force a confession, and left him tied to a tree in front of the Fort Valley guardhouse. The episode reached the press only as the reported cause of a threat to burn Fort Valley, and the local paper that described it said its only evidence was the prisoner's own statement.
